title: Consumer Protection Act — Organisational Complaint Receiving and NCC Compliance Process Flow
subtitle: Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 (“CPA”) · Consumer Protection Act Regulations, 2011 (GN R.293), as amended by the Consumer Protection Act Amendment Regulations, 2026 (GN R.7380, Government Gazette 54521, in force 15 April 2026) · Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (“POPIA”), s.69 · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells a supplier what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment a consumer complaint arrives — through any of the channels the CPA allows a consumer to use — until the matter closes and lessons feed back into controls. It runs alongside a second, non-case-triggered obligation that the 2026 Amendment Regulations put beyond doubt: registering as a direct marketer on the National Consumer Commission’s (“NCC”) opt-out registry, identifying the organisation in every marketing communication, and cleansing the marketing database against the registry every month. The two are related but distinct: a mishandled complaint exposes the organisation to a compliance notice, a Tribunal referral and an administrative fine of up to R1 million or 10% of annual turnover; unregistered or uncleansed direct marketing exposes it to the same fine once the NCC’s registration deadline (end-December 2026) has passed and full enforcement has begun (15 April 2027), independently of any single complaint.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The CPA is the binding law; the Consumer Protection Act Regulations, 2011 fill in prescribed forms, timeframes and procedure, and the 2026 Amendment Regulations are already in force. They were made under s.120(1)(a), read with s.11(6), of the CPA, and s.6 of the schedule states plainly that they “come into effect on publication date of the Notice” — 15 April 2026. The NCC’s April 2026 statements pointed to operational registration from July 2026; the registry opened for direct-marketer registration on 15 September 2026. On 7 October 2026 the NCC announced a phased roll-out: direct-marketer registration by end-December 2026; list cleansing December 2026–April 2027; consumer blocks from May 2027; full enforcement from 15 April 2027. Draft Opt-Out Registry Guidelines were published for comment on 2 October 2026 (GG 55465, Notice 7981); the comment period was extended to 6 November 2026. Register now; diarise these dates in steps 0.4 and 0.8 and step 6.6. POPIA applies in parallel to any electronic direct marketing and is enforced separately by the Information Regulator.

notes.heading: POPIA

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: A consumer can reach the system through several doors: directly to the organisation, to the ombud with jurisdiction over the organisation (the ordinary route where one exists, s.69(b)), to the NCC by lodging the prescribed Annexure E complaint form where no such ombud applies (s.69(c), s.71(1)), or in limited cases directly to the National Consumer Tribunal (“NCT” or “Tribunal”, s.69(a)). s.69(d) refers to approaching a court once other national-legislation remedies are exhausted, but the SCA (Motus v Wentzel, 2021) and later High Court authority (Pure Silk Invest v Martin, WCHC 2025) hold that it does not lightly exclude a consumer’s right to sue directly. Treat any summons or letter of demand as live from day 0 (step 1.3) and refer it to LA; do not assume a court will decline it. Because the organisation cannot control which door a complaint arrives through, this flow gives every channel the same single intake, so that the file, the evidence and the internal clock are identical whichever door was used.

notes.heading: Eight interpretation points that shape the flow
Counting days
notes.text: The CPA is not consistent: some provisions state “business days” expressly (the s.16 cooling-off period: 5 business days to cancel, 15 business days to refund, which does not apply where ECTA s.44 governs an online transaction; the s.101(1) compliance-notice objection window: 15 business days; the 40–80 business day automatic-renewal notice). Others, such as the s.116 three-year time limit, run in ordinary years. Where a provision is silent on the kind of day, the Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4 applies: calendar days, excluding the first and including the last, unless the last day is a Sunday or public holiday. Diarise every deadline by its own stated unit; do not assume business days as a default.

notes.heading: The consumer’s routes are structured, but every door is logged
notes.text: Section 69 sets out the consumer’s routes. Where the organisation is subject to an ombud with jurisdiction (e.g. CGSO, MIOSA, the NFO), that ombud is the ordinary route (s.69(b)). The provincial consumer court, ADR and NCC complaint routes under s.69(c) apply where it is not; s.71(1) ties NCC complaints to that route, and the NCC usually refers a matter to ADR or the accredited ombud unless that has already failed (s.72(1)(b)). A direct Tribunal referral (s.69(a)) applies only where the Act permits it; the court route is dealt with in the design principle above. The organisation must still accept and log a complaint through any door, and may respectfully point the consumer or the NCC to the ombud with jurisdiction.

notes.heading: The R2 million threshold
notes.text: The CPA protects a juristic person whose asset value or annual turnover, at the time of the transaction, is below the threshold determined by the Minister under s.6 for s.5(2)(b): currently R2 million (GN 294, GG 34181, 1 April 2011). It has not been revised since, although s.6 requires review at least every five years; check for a new determination at each annual review (step 6.6). Version 1.0 of this flow wrongly gave the figure as R3 million, citing Government Gazette 33621 (October 2010), which contained only the proposed determination; GBS materials that say R2 million are correct (see section 15, correction 1).

notes.heading: “Cleanse AND consent”, not “cleanse OR consent”
notes.text: POPIA s.69 governs whether the organisation may send an electronic direct-marketing communication at all (consent, or the existing-customer exception in s.69(3), plus an opt-out on every message). The CPA opt-out registry governs a separate, absolute question: whether a specific consumer has registered a pre-emptive block, in which case the organisation may not market to them regardless of any POPIA consent on file, and must remove their data by the next monthly cleanse. Both regimes must be satisfied for the same email, SMS, WhatsApp message or call.

notes.heading: Sector carve-outs
notes.text: Not every consumer complaint against the organisation is a CPA/NCC matter. Financial products and services (banking, credit, long- and short-term insurance) are generally handled by the National Financial Ombud Scheme South Africa (“NFO”), which since 1 March 2024 has replaced the Ombudsman for Banking Services, the Credit Ombud and the long- and short-term insurance ombuds; the National Credit Regulator remains the NCA regulator. Motor-industry disputes usually run through the Motor Industry Ombudsman of South Africa (“MIOSA”); electronic communications complaints may sit with ICASA. Screen every complaint at intake for a sector carve-out before assuming the CPA/NCC route applies.

notes.heading: Compliance notice or prosecution, never both
notes.text: Where the NCC issues a compliance notice under s.100 and the organisation disregards it, the Commission must choose between applying to the Tribunal for an administrative fine and referring the matter for prosecution under s.110(2); it may not do both for the same notice. On the fine route the Tribunal may impose up to the greater of R1 million or 10% of annual turnover (s.112); on the prosecution route the offence under s.110(2) carries a fine or up to 12 months’ imprisonment, or both (s.111(1)(b)). Either is serious, and the route chosen shapes how the organisation responds once a notice is contested.

notes.heading: The three-year clock (s.116)
notes.text: A complaint may not be referred to the Tribunal or a consumer court more than three years after the act or omission that caused it, or, for a continuing course of conduct, more than three years after that conduct ceased. A complaint outside this window is a ground for the NCC to issue a notice of non-referral (s.72(1)(a)) — but a complaint received near the edge of the window should still be logged and assessed, not assumed time-barred.

notes.heading: Provincial consumer protection authorities are uneven
notes.text: Section 84 lets a province operate its own consumer protection authority, able to issue compliance notices on the Commission’s behalf for conduct confined to that province, mediate disputes and refer matters to a provincial consumer court. All nine provinces nominally maintain an office, but their operational capacity varies considerably and a complaint referred there can sit for longer than one referred to the NCC directly. Treat a provincial referral as a live channel to track, not a channel to rely on for a fast outcome.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: CPA Compliance Officer (CO, the process owner and spine); Customer Service or Complaints Handler (CS); Marketing or CRM Administrator (MKT); Legal Adviser (LA); Finance (FIN); IT; Senior Sign-off (SSO, e.g. COO or Head of Compliance); Board or Risk / Social and Ethics Committee (BOARD). External: National Consumer Commission (NCC); accredited industry ombud, most commonly the Consumer Goods and Services Ombud (OMBUD/CGSO); National Consumer Tribunal (NCT); provincial consumer protection authority (PCPA); National Financial Ombud Scheme South Africa (NFO) or other sector ombud (SECTOR OMBUD); Information Regulator (IR); National Prosecuting Authority (NPA); the consumer or complainant (CONS).

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger: it must be in place before the first complaint or the first marketing communication, because the organisation’s exposure on both fronts is decided by controls that must already exist. An organisation that has not registered as a direct marketer risks non-compliance once the NCC’s registration deadline (end-December 2026) passes, and is exposed to enforcement from 15 April 2027; an organisation with no complaints process cannot produce the evidence trail the substituted Annexure E complaint form now expects of a consumer’s “steps already taken to resolve the complaint”.

notes.heading: Consumer side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed yet, but the consumer’s eventual routing depends on this phase: an organisation with no visible complaints channel or ombud membership pushes consumers straight to the NCC or the Tribunal, where the substituted Annexure E form now expects a documented account of “steps already taken to resolve the complaint” that the organisation had no opportunity to take.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A lapsed NCC registration or a missed monthly cleanse is usually discovered only when a complaint or an NCC inspection surfaces it. Check registration and cleansing status monthly, not only when a complaint arrives.

steps.title: Warranty and returns operations

stages.title: Phase 1 — Receipt and intake
intro: The clock starts on the day the organisation, an ombud, or the NCC first has notice of the complaint, not when the compliance officer first reads it. Day 0 is the day of receipt.

notes.heading: Consumer obligations at this stage
notes.text: None yet under the CPA itself, beyond providing enough detail to identify the transaction and the complaint; the substituted Annexure E form later expects the consumer to show what they did at this stage, so a clear, dated acknowledgement protects the organisation as much as it serves the consumer.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CS or any recipient → CO (same day). CO → LA (sector carve-out, external-channel arrivals). CO → IT (evidence preservation).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A complaint dismissed informally at the front line, with no C01 entry, leaves the organisation unable to show the “steps already taken to resolve the complaint” that the 2026 Annexure E form now requires a complainant to describe — and by implication, that the NCC now expects a supplier to be able to corroborate.

steps.title: Recognise and forward
steps.trigger: A consumer complains by any channel: call centre, email, social media, in-store, a letter of demand, or a sales representative is told directly.
steps.action: Forward to the CO the same day without argument or informal dismissal.
points: Forward to the CO the same day without argument or informal dismissal.

steps.title: Log and reference
steps.action: Open a case file; assign a reference number; record date, time, channel, complainant details, and a verbatim or near-verbatim account of the complaint.

steps.title: Recognise an external-channel arrival
steps.trigger: Complaint arrives as an ombud notification, an NCC notice of investigation, a compliance notice, a Tribunal application, or a summons or letter of demand, rather than directly from the consumer.
steps.action: Treat the external document as day 0 for that channel’s own clock (see section 12); open or link to the existing case file if one exists; brief LA immediately. A summons or letter of demand is live from day 0: do not assume a court will decline it under s.69(d).

steps.action: Send a written acknowledgement: reference number, what happens next, expected timeline, a named contact. Where the organisation is a CGSO participant, note that the CGSO generally expects the supplier to have had 15 business days to resolve the complaint before it accepts escalation.

steps.title: Evidence preservation
steps.trigger: Complaint concerns a product, service or transaction still traceable in company systems.
steps.action: Preserve purchase records, contracts, correspondence, call recordings and any defective goods; do not allow routine deletion cycles to run over evidence.

stages.title: Phase 2 — Triage and route determination
intro: By internal day 5 the organisation should know what kind of CPA matter this is, whether it is genuinely a CPA matter at all, and which of the s.69 routes the consumer has used or is likely to use next.

notes.heading: Consumer obligations at this stage
notes.text: Provide any further information reasonably requested to allow the complaint to be assessed; a consumer who has already engaged an ADR agent or ombud should say so, since the Annexure E form later asks for exactly that history.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CO → LA (applicability, classification). CO → FIN (exposure). CO → SSO (escalation trigger).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Do not let “the consumer is being difficult” substitute for a documented merits assessment. A Tribunal or an ombud tests the organisation’s conduct against the Act, not against the consumer’s tone.

steps.title: CPA applicability check
steps.action: Confirm the transaction falls within the CPA (consumer, or juristic person under the R2 million threshold); confirm no exclusion applies (e.g. transactions before 31 March 2011, certain credit-agreement or employment matters).

steps.title: Merits and exposure assessment
steps.action: Assess the strength of the complaint on the facts; estimate exposure (refund, repair, replacement, reputational, and — if the matter could reach the Tribunal — administrative fine risk under s.112); flag any pattern of similar complaints.

steps.title: Assign owner and target date
steps.action: Assign an internal owner for resolution; set an internal response target proportionate to complexity (BP 10 business days for straightforward matters, noting the CGSO generally allows the supplier 15 business days before escalation; longer with reasons recorded for complex ones).

stages.title: Phase 3 — Internal resolution
intro: The CPA does not compel a supplier to resolve every complaint internally before a consumer may go elsewhere, but a genuine, well-documented attempt is the organisation’s best evidence at every later stage, and CGSO and most industry codes expect it as a condition of membership.

notes.heading: Consumer obligations at this stage
notes.text: Engage with the process in good faith; provide requested evidence; a consumer who escalates without engaging internally is entitled to do so under s.69, but the organisation’s own record of a genuine offer remains relevant to any later assessment by an ombud, the NCC or the Tribunal.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CO → LA (contract/warranty review). CO → Ops, FIN (remedy delivery). CO → external escalation track (impasse).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A remedy offered only after the consumer has already gone to the NCC or an ombud is still worth making — it can narrow or resolve the matter — but is weaker evidence of good faith than an offer made promptly at first contact.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.action: Gather facts: transaction records, product or service history, prior complaints, staff accounts. Interview relevant staff where conduct (e.g. a verbal sales commitment) is in dispute.

steps.title: Legal or technical review

stages.group: Phase 4 — External escalation: ombud, NCC and Tribunal
stages.title: Phase 4 — External escalation: ombud, NCC and Tribunal
intro: Once a matter leaves internal resolution, it can run through several routes at once or in sequence, and each has its own procedure and clock. This phase is organised by the escalation event, not by a single linear timeline.

notes.heading: Consumer obligations at this stage
notes.text: Use the prescribed form and manner for the route chosen (Annexure E for an NCC referral); disclose prior ADR or ombud engagement and provide the closing letter where one exists; respect the s.116 three-year limit for referring the matter to the Tribunal or a consumer court.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CO → LA (every escalation event). LA → the Commission, the Tribunal, or the relevant ombud (formal responses). SSO → BOARD (fine exposure, reputational escalation).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A compliance notice and a prosecution referral cannot both proceed on the same notice (s.100(6), s.110(2)) — the fine route carries the s.112 ceiling and the prosecution route a fine or up to 12 months’ imprisonment, or both (s.111(1)(b)); either is serious, so contesting or complying promptly is usually the safer course once LA has assessed the notice’s validity.

steps.title: Ombud referral

steps.action: Respond to the ombud’s request for information within its stated timeframe; cooperate with mediation or conciliation; keep LA briefed on any proposed settlement. The GBS materials compress three distinct duties — being identifiable even on public platforms, not disseminating communications from an unidentifiable public-platform origin, and ensuring a communication transmitted to a recipient’s device is identifiable by the recipient — into a single “ensure communications are identifiable” line. Keep the compressed language for training purposes, but the compliance checklist and any audit tool should test all ten paragraphs separately, each mapped to one duty and to steps 0.4–0.8 and D1–D6 using the paragraph letters in the Gazette text (GN R.7380, GG 54521) (verify letters before building the tool).
The NCC established “under section 85” of the CPA
Correct: the NCC is established by s.85 of the CPA. No change needed.
Provincial escalation and “other regulators” not addressed at all

Add the s.84 provincial consumer protection authority route and the sector carve-outs (financial services, including credit, to the NFO, which since 1 March 2024 has replaced the Credit Ombud and the banking and insurance ombuds; NCA regulatory matters to the NCR; motor industry to MIOSA; electronic communications to ICASA) to the intake and escalation process; a complaint wrongly assumed to be an NCC/CGSO matter can sit unresolved with the wrong regulator.
No mention of the s.116 three-year time limit, the s.100–101 compliance-notice mechanism, the s.74 consent-order mechanism, or the s.112 administrative fine as the operative Tribunal remedy
These sit at the centre of NCC enforcement practice and are added throughout this flow (sections 4, 7, 8, 13 and 14).
“Administrative penalty risk” framed only as a consequence of the 2026 direct-marketing regime
Training Paper Module 1, Slide 1.5; Slide deck, Slide 2

The s.112 fine (the greater of R1 million or 10% of annual turnover) is the CPA’s general enforcement remedy, available for any confirmed prohibited conduct, not only direct-marketing non-compliance. Present it as the Act’s standing enforcement ceiling, with direct marketing as one route to it.
Annexure E summarised only as requiring “a documentary evidence trail”
Training Paper Module 5, FAQ D; Slide 10

The substituted Annexure E specifically asks whether the complaint was previously filed with the NCC (with reference number), whether it went through an ADR process (with the closing letter), the nature of the complaint, supplier details, a description, the steps already taken to resolve it, and the outcome proposed. Build the organisation’s own complaints file to answer each of these fields, not only “keep evidence”.
“Cleanse or consent” tension between regulation 4(3)(g) and regulation 4(7)(i) flagged as unresolved
CPA/POPIA compliance paper, “Cleanse or consent?” section

On the gazetted text read in this review, regulation 4(3) subparagraphs (i), (j) and (k) were deleted by the 2026 amendment (item 4(c) of the Schedule), and the operative rule is now regulation 4(7)(h)–(i) alone: no marketing to a blocked consumer, and monthly removal of blocked data. There is no longer a live drafting tension between two surviving sub-regulations on this point; the “cleanse and consent” conclusion in the paper remains correct, but the stated legal basis for the tension should be corrected.

intro: The definition of “electronic communication recipient”, inserted into regulation 1(2), means “a consumer who receives electronic communication from the direct marketer and has registered a pre-emptive block”. Regulation 4(7)(c) and (g), however, use that defined term to describe the general duty to make the marketer identifiable to any recipient and to ensure any communication is identifiable on the recipient’s device — duties that only make sense if they apply to every recipient, not only those who have already opted out. Read literally, paragraphs (c) and (g) apply only to consumers who have already registered a block, which cannot have been the intended scope. Treat the identification duties as applying to every recipient as a matter of policy pending clarification, and flag this for any formal comment the organisation or its industry body makes to the Department.

Annexure E is headed “Form – Complaint – Section 71(1)”, but nothing in the gazetted amendment states what happens if a complainant cannot supply a required field (for example, no ID or passport number, or no ADR closing letter because no ADR process was used). The form’s asterisked “required” fields are not matched to any stated consequence of omission in the text made available for this review.

Regulation 4(9)(b) requires a consumer to “ensure that their information kept in the opt-out registry is always up to date”, but no corresponding organisational or Commission duty compels a periodic reminder to consumers to do so, beyond the Commission’s general website-information duty in regulation 4(10)(d). A registry error caused by a consumer’s own stale information is a live risk the organisation cannot fully control for.
